A 0.10.0 machine pairs in inherit, or switches to it, only with a receiver whose well-known file says `control.inherit: true`; it tells everyone else's person "… doesn't know inherit mode yet; it would show this machine as safe". Set the flag once you show the mode truthfully and accept it in `/pair` and `/hello` (conformance `delivery/23`).
  - **Refusal code `mode` is now `permission`**, plus `refused` `model` and `failed` `model`. Map both codes; a 0.9.0 machine still says `mode`.
  - **Hello:** `start` (per harness: `permissions` among `read`, `safe`, `edits`, `auto`, capped by the mode; the default `permission`, which may be `inherit`; `models`, `any_model`), `prompt_files: true`, and no `home`: a start's `cwd` may be `~` or `~/…` instead. `harnesses` lists at most 20, and `modes` include `api` when an ACP agent is listed.
  - **Acks:** a start's `taken` and `delivered` carry `applied` (`permission` may be `inherit`). Show `applied`, never what was asked.
  - **Events:** `session.attended`, `turn.ended.background`, `turn.started.submitted_by` and `injected`, `session.launched_by`, and `account_id` `api-<16 hex>` for a Claude Code home on another API, named in `accounts[]` by `name` with no `email`. All optional, tier 0.
  - **ACP agents** (gemini-cli, opencode, goose, cursor, copilot-cli, droid and more) appear in `harnesses` and in ack `session` refs, acked in mode `api`; they take no start options.
  - **Device keys:** an app that can't run WebAuthn signs with a hardware-held P-256 key, `{id, alg: -7, spki, type: "device", store: "hardware", uv: "each-use"}`, its signature `{cred, sig}` (plus `str` in a grant) where an assertion would stand; a 0.10.0 machine says `key_types: ["passkey","device"]` when pairing and in every hello. To accept them, store and carry the key whole (all six fields) in a pairing's and a `key.add`'s `key`, pass a `{cred, sig}` grant, confirm or pairing proof through untouched, and say `control.signing.key_types: ["passkey","device"]` in your well-known file. They are added only as passkeys are: at the terminal's pairing code, or by a `key.add` a trusted key signed. A receiver that doesn't know them keeps working, passkeys only.
  - **While machines run 0.9.0:** send `permission` or `model` only where the last hello's `start` advertises them (0.9.0 ignores them silently); `files` on a `prompt` only with `prompt_files: true` (0.9.0 refuses them); a `~` folder only to a machine whose hello has `start`; never `inherit` as a command's level; a device key only for a machine whose last hello lists `device` in `key_types` (0.9.0 would store it as a passkey and refuse its signatures); read an absent `attended`, `background`, `submitted_by`, `injected` or `launched_by` as unknown, never as false, 0 or a person.
- a6f8bb7: A control `prompt` can carry `files`, as a `start` can (CONTROL.md §3.1, §6 `prompt`), to a machine whose hello says `prompt_files: true`. The daemon fetches and checks them as for a start, writes them to `<cwd>/.sessionpipe/files/<session>/<nonce>/` (the command's signed nonce, never the receiver's unsigned message id), and appends the same "Attached files" block before the message is handed over in any mode: a resume, a fork, a held SDK session, an ACP agent (`api`), a waiter or a Stop. A file that fails is acked `failed` with code `file` and the message is not delivered. A receiver no longer needs to put a link to an image into the message's text.
- d51fd31: `session.attended` says whether a person attends the session: an optional tier-0 boolean in the harness's own word, absent when the harness does not say (unknown, never `false`). Claude Code fills it from `CLAUDE_CODE_SESSION_ATTENDED`, counting a control turn and a session with a link (its Remote Control bridge, the desktop app) as attended: every headless run says `0`, a Remote Control session included, and a `claude -p` started inside one inherits `CLAUDE_CODE_ENVIRONMENT_KIND=bridge`, so the link is what tells them apart. The hook carries `CLAUDE_CODE_SESSION_ATTENDED` and `SESSIONPIPE_CONTROL_JOB` into the job, and the worker takes those and `CLAUDE_CODE_HOST_SESSION_ID` from the job alone, so a worker another session's hook spawned no longer lends a swept job its own. Codex, Gemini CLI, Antigravity and Devin leave it absent.
- fae77a5: `session.launched_by`: the session that started this one, as `<harness>:<id>`, read from `SESSIONPIPE_LAUNCHED_BY` in the hook's environment (PROTOCOL.md §3). A script that runs `claude -p` for a session sets it, and a receiver can group the run under its launcher without reading it as a subagent. A subagent keeps its `parent_id` and gets no `launched_by`.
- bd49ef7: A control `start` can say how much the new session may do and which model it runs (CONTROL.md §2, §3.1, §5 step 8, §6 Options; ADAPTERS.md "Start options"). `permission` is one of four levels, `read`, `safe`, `edits` and `auto`, with nothing above `auto`; `model` is the harness's own id, passed as one argument. The machine's `mode` is the ceiling, and a start above it, or at a level the harness has no flag for, is refused `permission` before anything is taken or run (the daemon's old `mode` code). On a machine in `inherit` mode a start that names no level runs with no permission flag, as the person's own sessions there do, and one that names a level may name only `read` or `safe`, since sessionpipe can't rank the person's own default; `inherit` is never a level a command names. The hello advertises what each harness takes here (`start`, capped by the mode: Claude Code's levels from its `--help`, Codex's models from its own cache; a harness's default may be `inherit`). A start's `cwd` may be `~` or `~/…`, read under the daemon user's home, so a receiver can start a session in a folder an event reported without the machine ever telling it its home. A start's level and model are recorded with the session, and every later resume or fork runs at the narrower of that and the machine's mode then (at most `safe` on an inherit machine for a session that named a level). The `taken` and `delivered` acks of a start carry `applied` (its `permission` may be `inherit`); a model the harness rejects ends `failed` with code `model`. An ACP agent takes neither option: a start that names one is refused, never run without it. Each command kind now has a closed set of fields, so a field a machine doesn't know is refused rather than ignored. `sessionpipe control status` shows the options per harness. A start whose text begins with a dash no longer reaches `claude -p` as a flag.
- d7269b4: `turn.ended` carries `background`: how much background work the harness reports still in flight as the turn ends, each piece of which wakes the session when it finishes. Claude Code's Stop hook lists it as `background_tasks` (in every Stop recorded since 2.1.258): a background shell command, a monitor, a subagent, a workflow. A session that ended its turn waiting on a two-hour background command read as finished on its receiver, under "Last 24 hours", until the command woke it. Tier 0, a count only: never what that work runs.
- f8770b9: `turn.started` can now say who started the turn: two optional tier-0 fields, `submitted_by` (the harness's own word for who submitted the prompt, forwarded verbatim and never mapped onto a vocabulary of the spec — a different vocabulary from `session.started.source`) and `injected` (`true` when the prompt text is a block the harness wrote rather than words a person typed). Claude Code fills `submitted_by` from `UserPromptSubmit.source` when a payload carries that key — its hook schema documents `user` · `sdk` · `system` · `loop_wakeup` · `schedule_wakeup` · `poll_event` and says a payload may omit it while the field rolls out, and no build through 2.1.304 sends it — and sets `injected` from a closed list of its own prompt wrappers (`<task-notification>`, `<cross-session-message …>`, `<system-reminder>`, `<local-command-stdout>`, `<command-…>`), so a task notification, a peer message or a slash-command expansion is distinguishable from a person typing. `injected: true` says only that the prompt is not the person's words, never that no person caused the turn: a Talk or `sessionpipe wait` delivery arrives inside a `<task-notification>`. Both fields are absent when the harness does not say, and an absent field is unknown, never "the person". `sessionpipe tail` prints both. Codex, Gemini CLI, Antigravity and Devin leave both absent.

## 0.9.0

### Minor Changes

- 55320c7: Control: `sessionpipe-core/control` accepts `files` on a `start` (1–10 files, each `{name, type, size, sha256}`, 25 MiB each, 50 MiB together, names safe to write and unique ignoring case) and refuses them on any other kind, `null` or empty as `bad_fields`; new exports `filesProblem`, `ControlFile` and the limits. Schemas: `control-command` gains `files`, `control-pair` / `control-hello` / the well-known `control` object gain `files: true`. 24 new shared vectors (`66`–`89`).
- d525320: A `devin` adapter: Devin CLI (Cognition) sessions are reported like any other harness. `sessionpipe install` (or `--devin`) writes the eight event names Devin accepts into the `hooks` key of its user config file; the payload maps to the protocol's events, the folder comes from `DEVIN_PROJECT_DIR` (nothing in the payload names it), and tier 2, the model, the title and the times are read read-only from Devin's own SQLite session store — through a new `readers/sqlite.ts` that works on Node 20 too (in-process `node:sqlite`, else a short child process, else the `sqlite3` CLI, else no turns). Eight fixtures recorded from real runs on 3000.11.3. Also: the `claude-code` adapter now drops a payload with no `transcript_path` and a non-UUID session id — that is another harness running our entry in `~/.claude/settings.json`, not Claude Code — and the worker logs a dropped event instead of discarding it in silence when no adapter owns its harness name.
- 3fd0041: Review fixes to the Devin adapter and two gaps it exposed.
  
  `devin`: a turn is now timed by the message's own `metadata.created_at`, not by `message_nodes.created_at` — that column is the time the row batch was last **saved**, one value for the whole chain, rewritten on every save and not monotonic along it, so every turn of a session was reported at the same wrong instant. The chain read is now bounded by the cursor and caps from the newest end: past 4000 nodes the old query kept the 4000 **oldest** and then delivered nothing ever again, and every Stop re-read the chain's root (a 17 kB system prompt and four more system blocks). `installed()` reports `inactive`, not `current`, when the config file holds any event name Devin does not know — Devin then loads no hooks from that file at all, ours included — and `install()` says so too. A `tool_response` that is not an object no longer loses its output. `facts()` takes the hook's environment (new optional argument on the `Adapter` interface), so a job swept by a worker another harness's hook spawned still reads the right config and session store.
  
  `sessionpipe uninstall` takes the same `--<harness>` selection `install` has, removes the shared hook launcher only on a full uninstall, and refuses an all-harnesses uninstall when `SESSIONPIPE_CONFIG`/`SESSIONPIPE_STATE` point away from this machine while other harnesses would still be read from `$HOME` (pass `--all` to mean it). The hook forwards `XDG_CONFIG_HOME`, `XDG_DATA_HOME` and `APPDATA` in the job file, beside the per-harness variables already there. The control wait — up to 125 s on a `PermissionRequest` — now applies the same "this is not a Claude Code payload" test the worker does, so our entry in `~/.claude/settings.json` run by another harness returns at once. A payload no adapter claims is logged rather than dropped in silence.
  
  Tests: the Devin session-store tests build their fixture through the `sqlite3` binary where `node:sqlite` is absent, so they run on the Node 20 floor — where the `cli` engine is the only way into a database, and where all seven used to skip. Each engine is asserted where it works and skipped only for itself; `inlineParams` and the adapter's own chain query are covered.
- 40fb6e5: A session's short id (PROTOCOL.md §3): the first 8 hex digits of `sha256("sessionpipe.session:" + harness + ":" + id)`, what a person reads in a log line, a notification or a search box. Derived, never sent. Not a prefix of the id: Codex ids are time-ordered, and four of ninety on one machine shared their first eight characters. `shortId()` in core; the worker's log and the daemon's lines that name a session use it.
- 0940788: `turn.progress` (tier 2): a turn still running goes out as it runs, not only when it ends. The prompt is sent as the turn starts, then what the assistant has said so far, at most every 20 s on a tool call and only when it changed, under the number its `turn.transcript` will carry. Over 20 000 characters the reply keeps its end. A 21-minute turn used to show nothing on its receiver for 21 minutes.

### Patch Changes

- d5c7511: Treat a hook stdin that is JSON but not an object (`null`, a number, a string, an array) as no payload in every adapter. Such a stdin made `fromHook` throw on the first field it read, and the worker job for that hook died with it; it is now handled exactly like an empty stdin, so the hook reports nothing and the session carries on.
- 8184e2a: An Antigravity session in a git checkout now opens its own conversation from its link, not Antigravity's home. Antigravity keeps a git checkout's folder under `gitFolder` in `~/.gemini/config/projects/<id>.json` (`{ "gitFolder": { "folderUri": … } }`) and only a plain folder's at the top of the resource, so the session's project was never found for a repo: the link had no `?p=c/<conversation>?section=<project>`, or named an enclosing plain folder's project instead (6 of 8 projects on one machine, 2026-10-20).
- 91265cb: A busy session's events no longer wait 6 s and go back to the queue behind its own lock. A lock whose worker is gone (its 15 s deadline ended it without a release) is taken at once instead of after 5 min; a job polls for the lock every 50 ms instead of doubling its wait, so siblings can't keep taking it in between; and the sinks drain at once, so the lock is held for the slowest round trip, not the sum of them (33 re-queues in one day's log on a machine with three sinks, 2026-10-13).
- 366043f: Claude Code: a message the person sends while a turn is running now reaches `turn.transcript` and `turn.progress`. Claude Code records it as a `queued_command` attachment rather than a `user` record, so the transcript reader dropped it from tier 2.
- 94c1b2f: Skip the parent's replayed history in forked Codex rollouts when reading session
  facts and transcripts. Wait for an event naming the fork's own thread, preserve
  its original transcript timestamps and cursors, and leave its title unset until
  it contains a real user ask of its own.
- 81764cc: Codex: only the person's own threads become sessions.
  
  - An ephemeral thread is no longer reported: its hooks carry `transcript_path: null` and its notify finds no rollout. Codex Desktop runs its own background work this way (ambient suggestions and their safety review, a new chat's title), and so does `codex exec --ephemeral`. Each used to arrive as an untitled session with no turns, often with `/` as its folder.
  - A subagent's thread is no longer a session of its own. Its parent already reports it (`SubagentStart` / `SubagentStop`, its tool calls), so its notify and its rollout (backfill) report nothing. A fork the person made is still a session.
  - Inside a subagent, Codex sends the parent's `session_id` with the subagent's own rollout. That file is no longer read as the parent's transcript, so the parent's running turn (`turn.progress`) no longer shows a subagent's words.
  - Conformance: a harness fixture with an empty `expect` is a payload the adapter must report nothing for.
- 4213f4e: Internal cleanup: fallbacks no input could reach are gone from the adapters, the privacy filter, the secrets ruleset, the outbox reader and the ULID. No behaviour changes; the public API is unchanged.
- ace786d: Write an `ssh://git@host/owner/repo.git` origin as `host/owner/repo` in `session.repo`, the same as the `git@host:owner/repo.git` form of that remote. Before, the two spellings of one repository reached a receiver as two different repos.
- bea1cae: Internal: the home directory is read when a path is asked for, not when the package loads. A process whose HOME changes after import (a test with a sandbox home) gets the new one; no user-facing change.
- 1ca23ee: No hook event is lost to a worker's 15 s deadline, and none waits for an unrelated hook. A worker used to delete its job file before running it, so one ended mid-run (a sink that hung, a lock held out) took the event with it. A job is now claimed by renaming its file and the claim is released only once its events are in the outbox; a sweep gives a claim whose worker is gone back to the queue. A job the session's lock held out used to wait in the queue for the next hook's sweep, however long that took; a fresh worker now starts for it.
- 434d10c: A machine under a flood of hook events no longer floods its sinks. One worker drains the sinks at a time; the others leave their events in the outbox for it and it sends them in full batches of 50, so four busy sessions cost a request per batch, not per event. A sink that answered 429 is not tried again by any worker before its `retry-after`, and one that could not be reached waits 2 s · 10 s · 60 s · 5 min · 30 min, then every 30 min, as HTTP.md §2 has said all along (a machine with four busy sessions was refused 828 times in two minutes and had 5 192 jobs queued, 2026-10-14). The session's lock now covers only the append, not the round trips.
- cdb1dbf: Draining a large session file no longer re-reads the rest of it for every batch: a read takes 1 MB (more only for one event longer than that), not the remaining file up to 8 MB, and counts its offset per line rather than from the start. A 10 MB session drained in batches of 50 decoded 55 MB.
- 67cc4fc: Recover a session's seq counter when its file is empty or not a number (a crash between truncate and write leaves it empty). Before, the counter restarted at 0 and the receiver's deduplication silently dropped every later event of that session; now the next seq is read from the outbox file's last line, as it already was when the counter file was missing.
- dc14f84: `turn.progress`: a message absorbed by a running turn, and text the person never typed, no longer open a turn of their own. Claude Code reports a message sent mid-turn (the person's, another session's, a task notification) as a prompt carrying the running turn's id; its reading went out numbered as the next turn, which the transcript never delivers, so a receiver kept showing it, with an empty reply, instead of the running turn. Such a prompt now leaves the reading on the turn the transcript is in, and a task notification that starts a turn is not shown as its ask. `isInjected` also recognises a wrapper tag with attributes (`<cross-session-message from="…">…</cross-session-message>`).
- cb36e47: The stdout sink answers with a retry result when its writer fails (a closed pipe under `sessionpipe tail | head`), as the file and HTTP sinks do, instead of throwing out of `send()`.
- d4b085c: Stop the transcript cursor before a last line the harness is still writing. Before, a prompt whose line had no newline yet when the worker read the file was counted as read and never delivered, so the reply that followed arrived as a turn with an empty prompt. A complete last line without a trailing newline is still read.

### Changed

- The server's store reads its full events through a log it is handed (the session files on
  disk, as before, or events held in memory), and nothing it imports needs Node, so the same
  store can later run in the phone app's page. Nothing changes in what the GUI shows or keeps.
- Checking an incoming event's id and tier no longer loads sessionpipe-core's Node code for two
  rules: the receiver keeps a copy of them, and a test holds the copy to sessionpipe-core
  0.13.6, so it runs in a page too. Events are accepted and refused exactly as before.

### Fixed

- **`service install` restarts a receiver that is still running an older copy of itself.**
  After `npm i -g` put a new sessionpipe-gui over the old one at the same place, the
  service's file already named the new files, so `service install` said "already running
  0.7.2" and left the old process running the old code; the page, newer, then called
  routes that server did not have ("HTTP 404" under Settings › Data › spacesheep). It now
  restarts it and waits for this version to answer ("updating … 0.7.2 → 0.8.0"), on macOS,
  Linux and Windows. A receiver on the port that isn't the service's own (one started by
  hand while the service is down: its `run.json` names a pid that isn't the service
  manager's, or on Windows a command line that isn't the task's) is left alone, with a line
  that says so; a receiver that couldn't write its `run.json` counts as the service's when
  the manager says the service runs. When the new
  version doesn't come up after the old one was stopped, it says so on stderr and exits 4.
  An older sessionpipe-gui no longer quietly replaces a newer service that runs from
  somewhere else (the version read from the `package.json` beside the service's CLI): it
  says so and leaves it, unless `--downgrade`; nor a service that runs a developer's
  checkout (a folder with `server/cli.ts` or `.git` beside `dist/`). A re-install with other
  `--port`, `--state` or `--host` by the same CLI or a newer version works as before. One
  `service install` or `uninstall` runs at a time (the lock is
  `service-<label>.lock` in the default state folder, `~/.local/state/sessionpipe-gui`;
  a crashed run's is taken over), and a `bootout` that finds the job already gone counts as
  stopped. `--if-installed` acts on a service that is there, installs none, never moves one
  to an older version, and exits 5 where it did nothing.
- **A receiver reports the version it is running**, read once when it starts. It read
  `package.json` on every request, so one whose package was replaced under it answered
  `/api/ui/info` with the new version while it ran the old code, and nothing could tell it
  was stale. `service install` takes the version from `run.json` (written once, at start),
  so it also restarts a receiver of 0.8.0 or earlier that answers with the wrong one.
- **The desktop app brings an older receiver on this computer up to its own version,**
  downloading nothing without a click. An app that updated itself kept talking to the
  receiver it had, which still ran the version that installed it. Once per launch, when
  this computer's receiver (the one its `run.json` names) first connects and runs an older
  version than the app: where a `sessionpipe-gui` on PATH is at the app's version or newer,

  when `npx` can't download it (offline, GitHub blocked), or there is nothing that could,
  it changes nothing and says so. "Start sessionpipe" uses the CLI on PATH instead only
  where that can't make the service older (no service installed, or a CLI at least the
  version it runs). The app runs one install at a time. An install still downloading when

  Windows `npx` alone. One whose `sessionpipe-gui` has begun is never killed: the app stops
  waiting and says it is still finishing, keeps reading what it prints until it ends, and

- **In the app, an option the receiver is too old for says so** instead of the receiver's
  "HTTP 404". Settings › Data › "Use a spacesheep account" against a receiver older than

  know), and a version that isn't below the option's is left out of the sentence. A page

- The help and the authoring guides call what `view`, `skin` and `plugin link` make a link,
  not a symlink: on Windows it is a junction where a symlink needs Developer Mode.
- **On Windows, "Start sessionpipe" looks for Node only in absolute folders.** After PATH
  it tries folders under `ProgramFiles`, `APPDATA`, `LOCALAPPDATA` and `USERPROFILE`, and

  `%NVM_HOME%\nodejs`) was looked up from the folder the app was started in, so a
  `node.exe` under that folder could be the one it ran. Such a value is now left out, as a
  `.` on PATH already is (#101); `ProgramFiles` then reads as `C:\Program Files`.
- **`sessionpipe-gui service` on Windows starts `schtasks`, `taskkill` and PowerShell by their
  full paths** under `%SystemRoot%\System32`. They were started by bare name, which is looked
  for first in the folder the command is run from, so a `schtasks.exe` lying there would
  have been run in their place. The commands it tells you to type name them in full too.
- **A `!NAME!` in the state folder's path is kept** where the registry turns cmd's delayed
  expansion on: the Windows task now runs the receiver through `cmd /v:off`. Without it cmd
  puts a variable's value there when NAME is one that is set (`C:\data\!OS!\state` became
  `C:\data\Windows_NT\state`), and the receiver was started on another folder. A task that
  0.8.0 installed gets the new line the next time `service install` rewrites it (a new Node
  or package path, a changed option, or a receiver that is not running), or at once with
  `service uninstall` then `service install`. A 0.8.0 `sessionpipe-gui` does not know a
  task with the new line as its own: remove it with this version.
- **`service uninstall` on Windows takes the `\sessionpipe\` folder out of Task Scheduler**
  with its last task, where it left it there empty; one that 0.8.0 left goes on the next
  `service uninstall`. The folder stays while another task is in it, and where PowerShell
  is held to constrained language mode, which cannot remove it.
- **`config.json` is kept readable by you alone.** Node applies a write's mode only when it
  makes the file, so a `config.json` that already existed with looser bits (recreated at the
  shell's umask after deleting `uiKey` as SECURITY.md says, for example with
  `jq … > tmp && mv tmp config.json`, or copied back from a backup) kept them while it held
  the sink token and the UI key. The GUI now takes the group and other bits off before every
  write, as it already sets its TLS keys to 0600 when it writes them, and also when it
  starts; where that fails it says so and starts anyway.
- **A message that is held for you to confirm can be sent.** When spacesheep's safety check
  holds a message to a machine paired there, the page now says so where you sent it: the
  message, spacesheep's reason in its own words, and a "Confirm with your passkey" button. It
  goes only when you press that button; change the message first and the hold is dropped.
  It used to say "try again", and every try was held the same way, so such a message could
  not be sent from the GUI at all.
- **Child sessions stay under their parent when the GUI restarts.** A session started by
  another one (a subagent) was counted as its parent's child while the GUI ran, and every
  restart forgot it: the parent showed no children and the agent row for that child no
  longer opened the child's page, until the child sent something new.

### Added

- The receiver keeps three things a sessionpipe 0.13 machine says. `inbox` among a
  machine's delivery modes and as the mode of an ack, which it used to drop as a word it

### Fixed

- **A `session.seq` above 2^53 − 1 is refused**, the schema's bound: the receiver answers
  `bad_seq`, and the outbox reader and the demo drop it. Two such seqs in one session hung
  the GUI server at 100% CPU while it listed the hole between them; a store an older
  release already wrote them into now boots instead of hanging.
- **One session file the outbox can't read no longer stops the outbox.** A file the GUI
  may not open (its mode, another user's) or a folder named `*.jsonl` made the first read
  fail, and no session from the outbox reached the board while that file stayed so,
  restart or not; one that turned unreadable while running kept every older session from
  being read and the offsets from being saved, with a line on stderr every 500 ms. That
  file is now skipped for the tick, said once, and read on from its offset once it can be
  read again.
- **Setup's "Pair this machine" works on Windows.** The receiver ran `sessionpipe.cmd` through
  cmd.exe, which never handed its output back (the step sat at "Starting the pairing…") and
  split a folder with a space, such as `C:\Users\Ann Lee\code`, into two words. It now runs the
  script the npm shim names under its own node, with no shell, as it does on a Mac.
- **Setup speaks Windows.** On a Windows receiver the secure-address step pointed at
  `brew install openssl` and gave Debian and Fedora commands for trusting the certificate; the
  pair step's button said "Pair this Mac". It now names Git for Windows' openssl (or winget),
  gives `certutil -user -addstore Root ca.crt` and the Install Certificate… steps (also on the
  trust page and from `sessionpipe-gui tls trust`), and the button says "Pair this machine"
  off a Mac.
- A self-assigned 169.254 address (no DHCP answered on that link) no longer comes first among
  the receiver's LAN addresses, so the Machines page's pair command, Connect and the phone
  link name an address the other device can reach.
- **A virtual adapter no longer comes first.** Windows' "vEthernet (…)" switches (WSL 2,
  Hyper-V), VirtualBox and VMware host adapters, and Linux's libvirt, LXD, Incus, LXC,
  Multipass and Podman bridges sort after the real interfaces, whatever their case, so the
  phone's QR code, Connect and the `sink add` command name an address the other device can
  reach. No address is dropped: a Hyper-V external switch keeps the host's LAN address on
  "vEthernet (External…)", after any real-named interface.
- **`--host 127.0.0.1` (or `::1`, `localhost`) no longer offers LAN URLs nothing listens
  on.** The banner listed every LAN address as a `network` URL, its phone QR and the sink
  command pointed at one of them, and a bind to `::1` gave a sink command on `127.0.0.1`;
  all of them refused connections. A loopback bind now offers no LAN URL, and the sink
  command names the address it bound, under "from this machine"; a bind to one LAN
  address lists that address alone as its network URL.
- **A `config.json` that does not parse is never written over.** A `config.json` left empty or
  half-written by a write that died, or hand-edited so it no longer parses, was silently
  replaced with fresh secrets on the next start, so every sender paired with the old sink
  token got 401 and every phone and browser holding the old UI key was refused, with nothing
  said. The GUI now stops with a message that names the file and what to do, and leaves it
  byte for byte as it was; one it cannot read (a folder of that name, no permission) stops
  it the same way instead of with a stack trace. A `config.json` with a UTF-8 byte-order
  mark (PowerShell 5's `UTF8` encoding, older Windows editors) is read past it, instead of
  being replaced the same way. `sessionpipe-gui search` and `index` read the history setting
  past a byte-order mark too, and stop the same way on a `config.json` the GUI refuses,
  instead of reading it as history on.
- A plugin turned on with `sessionpipe-gui plugin enable` while the receiver runs starts
  on Reload plugins, as the CLI says. And a plugin or view the CLI turns on or off
  while it runs is no longer undone by the receiver's next write of config.json (a token
  rotation, a toggle in Settings, a spacesheep connect), which put back the lists it held
  in memory.
- **`npx github:spacesheep-dev/sessionpipe-gui` works on Windows.** Its one-time build
  spawned a bare `npm`, which is `npm.cmd` there and can't start without a shell, so the
  command exited 1 with no message. The build now runs npm through npm's own entry under the
  same node, and says why if npm can't be started. Its check for the build tools also looked
  for `@vitejs/plugin-react/package.json` through the package's exports, which leave it out,
  so on every platform the tools were installed a second time; on Windows that install ran
  the build script again, and again, until the PATH outgrew cmd.exe.
- **The desktop app on Windows tells a stale receiver from a live one.** It decides whether
  the receiver that wrote `run.json` still runs by its process id, and on Windows that check
  always said yes. It now asks Windows, so a file left by a receiver that has stopped is no
  longer taken for the one that dropped. The hand-run Desktop workflow also passes on
  `windows-latest`: its `npm ci` skips the prepare build, as desktop-release does, two tests
  no longer assume macOS, and the four that run a shell script are compiled on Unix only.
- **The desktop app's first-run sheet speaks Windows and Linux.** The New session shortcut
  reads Ctrl+Alt+N there (it read ⌃⌥N, the Mac's symbols, everywhere), as does the
  recorder in Settings › App; the sheet says sessionpipe is in your system tray, not your
  menu bar; and a refused notification points at Windows' Settings, not System Settings.
- **The desktop app's welcome and tray say "this computer" off a Mac.** On Windows and
  Linux the welcome offered to start sessionpipe on "This Mac" ("so this Mac's sessions show
  up here", "Nothing leaves this Mac"), and the tray listed an unreachable local receiver as
  "This Mac". A Mac still reads exactly as before.
- Search no longer says "“c:” isn't a filter" over a pasted Windows path (`C:\Users\…`,
  `D:/repo`) or a URL (`https://…`). They were, and still are, searched as text; the notice
  now stays for something that looks like a filter, such as `foo:bar` or `cwd:/x`.
- **The tier lens shows prompts, turn ends and attentions as a lower-tier receiver gets
  them:** under a lens below tier 3, who submitted a prompt (`submitted_by`, `injected`)
  and the background work still running when a turn ends (`background`) now stay, and an
  attention's `turn_id` and `call_id`, which the client never sends, go, as does its
  `agent_id` at tier 0.
- Board filters apply immediately even while focus or the pointer holds the row order.
- **Search shows a message just indexed at once when the indexer runs inside the server.**
  Where the indexer cannot be forked it runs in the server's own process, and there a
  request to commit that arrived while an earlier commit was being published was dropped:
  the new messages then waited for the timed commit, up to a minute. The forked indexer
  never dropped one.
- **Turning history search off works on Windows.** With Node 20, Settings › Data answered
  "internal", left the history index on disk and stopped the indexer until the GUI was
  restarted: the server still had that index open while it deleted it, which Windows
  refused. It now lets go of it first. If another program still holds a file of it, the
  setting is saved anyway, indexing goes on, and the status is an error naming the index
  left on disk until a later try (the indexer's next start, or Rebuild) deletes it.
- **A Windows file is listed once.** A full path from Claude Code on Windows
  (`C:\Users\…\acme\src\index.ts`, with either slash or the drive in another case) is shown
  relative to the session's folder, as `src/index.ts`, as on a Mac, so the Files drawer, the
  Review page and the changed-files count no longer give one file a row for each
  spelling of its full path.
- **`view`, `skin` and `plugin add` and `link` work on Windows.** A .zip is unpacked with
  the tar.exe Windows ships instead of failing with "unzip is not installed"; an npm
  package or a git URL runs npm's own script under the GUI's node instead of failing with
  "npm is not installed" while npm is on PATH; and `link` makes a junction where Windows
  refuses a symlink, so it no longer fails with EPERM when Developer Mode is off.
- **A finished session stays finished.** A sender records a hook when it gets to it, so a
  tool call that fired just before a turn's Stop can be recorded after it; the receiver
  read that late event as a new turn, and the session went back to "working" (then
  "stale") until its next prompt. An event from before the last end of the turn, or of the
  session, now takes nothing back: it is filed and counted, and the session stays idle or
  done. The same for an agent whose start is recorded after its end, and for the end of a
  run recorded after the session started again. Only an event timed within two seconds
  before that end is read so (the furthest a hook was found recorded behind, on a real
  machine, is 1.3 s). Further back than that it is the sender's clock that moved: a clock
  that stepped back, a session resumed where the clock is behind, or a batch from a clock
  ahead of the receiver's is read in the order it was recorded, so a running session never
  reads idle or done because of its clock.
- **A page that was away shows what is true now.** After the live stream dropped and came
  back, an open session page kept the events it had: a turn still drawn as running, a
  message still "handing it over", a reply missing, until a reload. The page now reads
  what it missed, once, when the stream is back, with nothing redrawn, the scroll where it
  was and the draft in the composer kept. A tab shown again after a long time hidden, a
  page restored by Back, a laptop awake again and a network that returned all ask for a
  fresh stream instead of trusting the old one, and coming back online no longer waits
  out a retry timer.
- While the stream is down a session page stops its spinners and its clocks where they
  were, as the board's rows do, and the page counts as live again when the fresh state
  has arrived, not when the connection opens: nothing reads as running, or can be sent
  or stopped, on what the page knew before.
- An event that arrived in the instant a session page finished loading no longer goes
  missing from its timeline.
- **One conversation, drawn once.** A message sent from a session's page and the turn it
  became are one block, in the cases where they were two or the wrong one. A message
  handed to a terminal session at its turn's Stop (sessionpipe 0.13.4) is its own exchange
  after that turn, "Turn 4, continued": it used to take the typed turn's place, so the
  typed prompt and its reply were gone, or, when that turn had begun over a minute
  before, to be drawn again at the end for two minutes. A prompt the machine scrubbed a
  secret, an email address or a phone number out of, and any message to a machine whose
  clock is behind, is its turn (both showed twice while the turn ran). A refused or
  expired message no longer takes a later turn that says the same words, which drew the
  refusal on a turn that ran; and a machine whose clock is ahead no longer hides it. The
  turn after one that was stopped keeps its own words, which were drawn on the stopped turn.
- **A stopped turn reads as stopped.** After Stop the turn stays where it was, with what
  it had written and a quiet "Stopped" where a running turn says "Running"; one stopped
  before it wrote anything says "Stopped before the first word.", and so does a message
  stopped before its turn began, which read "Delivered. Its turn shows here when it
  begins." The daemon's "(The turn was cancelled.)" and Claude Code's "No response
  requested." are never shown as what the agent said, a turn stopped at its terminal no
  longer shows the raw word "interrupt" beside a duration that ran to the next prompt, and
  a tool call the stop cut off no longer spins.
- **The desktop app's "Start sessionpipe" finds Node on Windows.** It looked through a login
  shell and for `node` and `npx` in Homebrew, nvm and Volta folders only, so on Windows it
  always said "sessionpipe needs Node 20 or later". It now reads the app's own PATH, then
  Program Files, `%APPDATA%\npm`, nvm-windows, Volta and Scoop; runs the scripts behind
  npm's `.cmd` shims under node; and starts them with no console window. It takes only the
  absolute folders of PATH, for the search and for the PATH it hands the installer, so a
  `.` there is never where it finds `node.exe`. The button then runs `sessionpipe-gui
  service install` (the scheduled task above) and opens the board. Opened again, the app
  finds the receiver on this computer (it looked for it only under HOME, which Windows
  doesn't set, and showed the welcome instead).
- **The Windows app's updater reads update archives with `zip` 9.5.1** (it was 4.6.1), which
  has the fixes for an archive whose two headers disagree writing files outside the update
  folder (GHSA-m665-v7pm-7grj, CVE-2026-115905), a symlink target that aborts extraction or
  exhausts memory (GHSA-q7v9-x93c-xqv3, CVE-2026-115909), and an AES entry passing its HMAC
  check when the file ends early (GHSA-8hxf-qr8p-62x4, CVE-2026-115906). It comes with
  `tauri-plugin-updater` 2.14.1, whose own code is unchanged. The macOS and Linux apps never
  read update archives with `zip`.

### Security

- **One request could stop the server.** A path whose percent escape does not decode as
  UTF-8 (`/api/ui/sessions/%E0%A4%A/x`) threw outside the request's error handling and
  ended the process, before any key was checked, so anyone who could reach the port could
  do it. It is now a `400 bad_path` and the server keeps serving. A cookie value that does
  not decode (another app on the same host can set one, since cookies ignore the port) is
  read as it is instead of failing every request from that browser. Upgrade if the GUI
  listens on your network (the default).

**Help says which refusals a command can give, and a refusal names its word.**

- `spacesheep <noun> <verb> --help` ends with the refusal words that call can give, one a line, each with what it means (from the server's table).
- The top-level `--help` lists the words any call can give, once.
- A refusal prints its word after the message: `✗ Space not found. (not_found)`. With `--json` the answer is unchanged.
- A server whose table carries no refusal words shows help as before.

Full list: https://github.com/spacesheep-dev/spacesheep-cli/pull/64

**A slow first answer from the server no longer looks like a broken command.**

- A command only the server's table can run (`spacesheep spaces list`) waits up to 12 s for that table on a fresh machine, instead of printing the general help after 5 s.
- If the table still doesn't come, the command says why (no answer in time, couldn't connect, a 5xx, a login page) and exits 1. A server without the table (404, 401, 403) runs today's commands as before.
- `versions list --space x` on a fresh machine goes through the table rather than looking for a space called "list".
- A cached table is used as it is for the server's `max-age`; after that, checking for a newer one waits at most 1.5 s.
- An empty list prints `No spaces.` rather than only `✓ done`.

Full list: https://github.com/spacesheep-dev/spacesheep-cli/pull/63

**Every server call is a command, and deploy never overwrites by accident.**

- `spacesheep <noun> <verb>` runs any call the server lists in `GET /v1/doors.json`, with its flags, `--help` and exit codes (0 answered, 1 refused or unreachable, 2 usage, 3 no key). A new server call needs no CLI update. `--json` prints the call's answer; a refusal prints its code, message and each `field: message`.
- A server without the table changes nothing: today's commands run as before. Where the server serves them, `list` and `versions <space>` run on the new calls, and `talk listen` and `sessions export` use them too. `deploy`, `read`, `share` and `delete` stay as they are.
- `deploy` sends the version this folder is built on (from its last publish or `read -o`), so a page someone else changed since is merged, or refused as a clash, rather than overwritten. `--base <sha>` names the version yourself; `--replace` replaces the live version on purpose. A clash offers keeping both first.
- `read -o` writes every file exactly, binary files included, or writes nothing, and records the version it read.
- `spacesheep mcp` names the harness and its version in its User-Agent.

Full list: https://github.com/spacesheep-dev/spacesheep-cli/pull/62

**Publish for a team on purpose.**

- `spacesheep deploy --team <name|slug|id>` puts a **new** space in one of your teams. `--team-access view|edit` sets what members may do (view by default). `--no-team` publishes personal.
- A repo can name its team once: put `.spacesheep.json` with `{ "team": "Acme" }` at the repo's root. The CLI looks at `--team` first, then the folder's own `.spacesheep.json`, then the nearest one above it, no higher than the repo root and never your home folder. There is never a default team.
- Every push prints `⌂ Lives in …`, Spacesheep's read-back of who can open the page.
- An update never moves a live space into or out of a team. If the folder names a different team, the CLI says nothing moved.
- A server older than `team` would drop it without saying so. The CLI catches that and says the page went out personal.

# Fortress v3 (Chromium 153.0.8010.36)

Fortress is a recompiled Chromium that corrects its own fingerprint in C++ (canvas, WebGL, WebGPU, audio, fonts, navigator, and 40 more surfaces) and exposes raw CDP, a drop-in for Playwright and Puppeteer. This release is the v3 engine, the offline license gate, and a new license.

## Highlights

- **A distinct machine every launch.** Each start mints a fresh, coherent persona across canvas, WebGL, WebGPU, audio, fonts, navigator, and hardware, verified 48 of 48 distinct across a clone fleet.
- **Recorded-human mouse motion.** A bank of real human cursor trajectories drives movement inside the engine, not a JavaScript overlay.
- **Widevine EME** on the Linux x64, Windows x64, and macOS builds for DRM playback.
- **Native per platform.** The same engine ships as a native binary for each OS, now including native Apple Silicon. A Windows build draws Windows personas (Win32, D3D11 GPUs), a Mac build draws Mac personas (Apple GPU, Metal), a real OS story a single host cannot fully emulate.
- **Free for developers, unlocked in one command.** `tilion activate` runs a browser sign-in that takes about ten seconds and saves your key to `~/.tilion/license.jwt`. The key is verified offline after that; Fortress never phones home or reports usage. Skip activation and it still runs, printing one notice and falling back to the public first-generation engine.
- **A new license.** Fortress moves from BSD to the Fortress Source Available License 1.1. Development, testing and evaluation stay free at any company size; production is free for individuals and for organizations under US$500,000 in cumulative funding and US$300,000 or less in ARR; every other organization buys one flat subscription.

## The `tilion` CLI

Installing the SDK (`pip install tilion-fortress` or `npm install tilion-fortress`) puts the `tilion` command on your `PATH`. The portable tarball and the Docker image bundle the same activator, so it works everywhere with no extra install.

```bash
tilion activate                 # unlock v3: opens your browser, sign in, done
tilion activate --headless      # SSH or remote host: prints the URL and code to enter
tilion activate --token <jwt>   # CI, Docker, agents: save a key with no browser
tilion license status           # show the saved key's tier and expiry
tilion license refresh          # re-issue the key before it expires
tilion license logout           # remove the key and drop back to v1
tilion get [platform]           # download the build for this host ('tilion get list' shows all)
tilion mcp                      # run the Fortress MCP server (stealth browsing as agent tools)
tilion                          # launch the engine and print the CDP endpoint
```

Activation captures a verified name and email through one click (GitHub, Google, or email) and saves the key to `~/.tilion/license.jwt`. Each developer gets a unique key that auto-refreshes, so you activate once. For a fleet with no browser (CI, Docker, agents), set `TILION_LICENSE_KEY=<key>` in the environment, or run `tilion activate --token <key>`; one key covers the fleet. A valid key runs the full v3 engine; with no key Fortress runs the public first-generation engine after a single notice.

# Fortress 151.0.7908.0 — Engine Refresh · **Released**

The stealth Chromium engine, rebuilt. Every launch is a different, fully-coherent real-device persona — **compiled into Chromium's C++, not bolted on in JavaScript.**

## What's new
- **Per-locale keyboard** — `navigator.keyboard.getLayoutMap()` returns the persona's real country layout (QWERTY / QWERTZ / AZERTY), full length, coherent with the locale.
- **Per-persona media devices** — `enumerateDevices()` presents a coherent per-persona device set; no empty or host-leaking enumerations.
- **Coherence hardening** — a full delivery-parity audit closed the last surfaces where a value could be *read* but not *delivered*. Platform ↔ GPU ↔ timezone ↔ language ↔ voices ↔ keyboard now move as one.
- **Real-silicon-calibrated render family** — GPU / WebGPU surfaces validated against real consumer hardware.

## Why it's different — the methodology
Fortress doesn't rewrite the fingerprint in JavaScript. It **compiles coherence into the browser itself.**
- **Native-code parity** — no JS wrappers, so `toString()` stays `[native code]` and every descriptor is untouched. The anti-instrumentation traps that catch script-injection stealth pass here *by construction*.
- **Realm-invariant** — one persona holds across the main frame, workers, service workers, and nested iframes. Detectors that diff the worker realm find nothing to diff.
- **One binary, per-launch personas** — a single build mints a different coherent device identity on every launch, zero config. No profile pool, no fingerprint to reuse.
- **Coherent, not random** — every surface is drawn from a real-device joint distribution, so a persona blends into the real-user crowd instead of flagging itself as "randomized."

## Built to resist reverse-engineering
The intelligence ships as **compiled machine code, not JavaScript** — no bytecode to deobfuscate, no readable fingerprint table to lift. The device-model corpus and the engine that mints personas are **not in the binary.** You get a browser that behaves like a real fleet; the *how* stays ours.

## Verified
**CreepJS 0% headless / 0% stealth** · **sannysoft all-green** · **Runtime.enable no-leak** · worker-realm coherent.

```
pip install -U tilion-fortress
docker run --rm -p 9222:9222 tilion/fortress:latest
```

## AAC compression attack

Thanks to @sarthakuwar for contributing `AacCompressionAttack` in #32 and refining it through review.

- Encodes with ffmpeg's built-in AAC-LC encoder and decodes back to PCM.
- Uses an `.m4a` container to account for encoder priming delay and preserves the input length.
- Defaults to a 64 kbps target bitrate, configurable with `bitrate_aac`.
- Included in `audio_editing` and the `compression_quantization` report subsection. Selecting all attacks or the audio-editing group now includes AAC.

No new AAC dependency is required beyond the existing ffmpeg requirement. Existing attack implementations are unchanged by the AAC addition.

## Maintenance

This release also includes Dependabot configuration and dependency updates from #38, #39, #40, and #41.

## Validation

All six AAC tests pass. The review suite recorded 933 passing tests on the AAC PR versus 927 on main, with the same three time-stretch/pitch golden failures in the review environment. Direct checks at 16 and 22.05 kHz confirmed sample alignment and preserved length. These checks do not validate every Docker service build.

AAC's canonical golden recording remains deferred; its documented exclusion is retained.

**Full changelog:** https://github.com/deepmark/deepmarkpy-benchmark/compare/v3.0.0...v3.1.0

**Measurement settings move from flags into one JSON config file per mode.** `--config` runs one or more of them, `--init <mode>` prints a commented template, and `--validate-only` checks a file against the discovered plugins without running anything. The validator reports every problem together, each with a stable code and its JSON path. Without `--config` the 2.x flags still run: they are assembled into a config and validated the same way.

### Added

- Per-group metrics and statistics: each attack group enables its own metrics and the statistics they are reported at.
- Per-version attack parameters (`AttackName:version`), including versions a config defines itself.
- Duration groups: a report part per audio-length bin.
- An `efficiency` section, off by default: embed, detect and attack latency, and the memory of the containers a run used.
- Attack-strength curves in the benchmark report: accuracy across an attack's versions.

### Changed

- `--save_audio` with several modes in one invocation, including `--no_attacks --detection_reliability`, writes each mode to `audio/<mode>/`.
- The detailed report is written on every run and holds tables only.
- `no_attacks` and the reliability baseline measure PESQ, ViSQOL and STOI without `--calculate_quality_metrics`, as benchmark mode always has.
- An unknown CrossModel second model (`E011`) and a `detection_reliability` model without `is_watermarked()` (`E044`) fail validation before anything runs.

### Breaking

- Removed `ReplacementAttack` and `Replacement2Attack`. No other attack's output changes.
- Each `metrics.<metric>` in `detection_reliability.json` is now an object of statistics rather than the mean.
- Attack parameter flags (`--snr_db_gaussian_noise`) must be spelled in full; 2.x accepted an unambiguous prefix.
- Exit codes: `1` when a mode produces no results, `2` for an invalid configuration or an unreachable model service (nothing runs). A skipped model or a report that fails to render is logged and still exits `0`.
- Internal Python APIs of `deepmarkpy.run`, `deepmarkpy.benchmark`, `attack_groups` and the report generators changed. The engine API in `docs/CONSUMING.md` did not.
- `tqdm` is no longer a package dependency.

**Attack outputs change. Results are not comparable with v1.x.** v1.x preserved the pre-package behavior bit-for-bit; this release is the deferred-fix release and corrects it deliberately.

### Behavior changes (why this is a major version)

Four attacks now produce different audio:

- **Equalizer** — filters were applied in parallel rather than cascaded, the band width formula inverted Q so every band was twice as wide, output was peak-normalized unconditionally, and two of the ten configured bands were never built.
- **Bandstop** — designed in transfer-function form, which lost enough precision at its 350–500 Hz band to reach ~1e147 output at 48 kHz. Now second-order sections.
- **PCM quantization and MP3** — nine float-to-int casts truncated toward zero instead of rounding, costing 6 dB of quantization noise and doubling the deadzone around silence.
- **Mixing** — passed `gains=` where the equalizer reads `gains_equalizer`, so its configured gains were silently ignored.

Four attacks are newly available: `WaveletAttack`, `PitchShiftAttack`, `TimeStretchAttack` and `InvertedTimeStretchAttack`. `pywt` and `pyrubberband` were undeclared, so they silently failed to load on a clean install — the benchmark reported 43 attacks where the paper promised more.

Two more corrections that change results only when they fire: a failing `InvertedTimeStretch` used to return its input, which scored as the detector's unattacked ceiling; and `ZeroCrossInserts` dropped the head of every file longer than one second.

### Transport

Audio crosses the HTTP hop as base64 of the raw float64 buffer rather than a JSON array of decimals: 20.9 → 10.7 bytes per sample in both directions, with no decimal formatting or parsing on either end. float64 is deliberate — float32 would halve it again but is lossy, and would move reported numbers. Verified bit-identical against the v1 fixtures. Services still accept the JSON list form.

### Security

- All 16 services publish on `127.0.0.1` only. They were bound to `0.0.0.0` and reachable from the LAN and any VPN interface, unauthenticated, exposing `/embed` and `/detect` as a watermark oracle.
- `speech_enhancement_2` validated `model_name` against ClearVoice's own model list. It was interpolated into a config path with no check, which made the endpoint a filesystem-existence oracle that returned YAML key names in its error body.
- Request audio is length-capped; every service had accepted an unbounded body.
- `timbrewm` loads its checkpoint with `weights_only`.

### Reliability

- Five service clients had no timeout and no status check; all ten now match.
- A null `audio` in a 200 response is an error naming the service, instead of becoming a 0-d object array that failed later somewhere unrelated.
- A requested attack that is not loadable raises instead of being skipped, and `--attack_groups` no longer silently drops attacks whose plugin failed to import — nor expands an all-failed group to the entire registry.
- Results are written after every file rather than only at the end.
- `.env` is loaded by the CLI, so a port set there reaches the host clients and not just Compose.
- `network_transmission` reports `netem_active`, so a run where the kernel impairment never engaged is no longer indistinguishable from one where it did.

### Reporting

- Metrics that cannot express what an attack did are marked and explained per-case rather than with one hard-coded sentence, in all three generators.
- `attack_snr_db` is recorded per file, making each attack's real strength visible — `additive_noise` sets an absolute amplitude, so its effective SNR moves with input level while its SNR-parameterized siblings hold constant.
- `AdditiveNoise`, `Replacement2` and `VAE` were in no attack group and fell through group resolution and report sectioning.
- NISQA's availability is recorded in `run_metadata.json`; its default weights path was broken by the src-layout move, so the documented setup produced nothing.

### Images

18.6 GB → 14.1 GB. `speech_enhancement_2` carried a full CUDA 13.0 stack on a CPU-only benchmark; `aware` duplicated a 411 MB torch tree for one patch version; `timbrewm` and `silent_cipher` shipped a torchaudio that could not be imported. The benchmark is CPU-only by decision, enforced by a test.

### Setup

`.env` is no longer tracked — it duplicated `.env.example` variable for variable, and being tracked while gitignored made every local port edit show up as a repo modification. **A fresh clone now needs `cp .env.example .env` before `docker-compose up`.** `HOST` stays `0.0.0.0`: it is uvicorn's bind address inside each container, and what keeps the services off the network is docker-compose publishing every port on `127.0.0.1`.

### Removed

- `docs/MIGRATION.md` (the v1.0.0 packaging migration).
- CI workflow, to be reintroduced in a later release.
- `.env` from version control; `.env.example` is the template.

Additive release: engine base classes and per-plugin engine names. No behavior, HTTP-contract, or CLI change — all 16 service contract fixtures re-verified byte-identically where deterministic.

- `deepmarkpy.core.inference` provides `BaseAttackEngine` (`apply`) and `BaseModelEngine` (`embed`/`detect`). The module is import-light (stdlib + numpy), so consumer serving code can be typed against the bases without any ML runtime installed.
- Every plugin engine now carries its own class name — `VAEEngine`, `AudioSealEngine`, `OpusCodecEngine`, and so on, mirroring the client class names — and derives from its family's base.
- Fully backward compatible: each `inference` module keeps `Engine` as a stable alias, so every v1.0.0 import path continues to work unchanged.
- The engine naming, base-class, method, and alias contract is locked by a structural test suite.
- Documentation: `docs/CONSUMING.md` lists the engine class per plugin and shows typing against the bases; the README covers the containerized plugin layout for both attacks and models, and its plugin-authoring paths now match the packaged tree.

First release of the `deepmarkpy` package. Behavior is bit-for-bit identical to the pre-package benchmark, verified by discovery lock tests, native-attack golden fixtures, and HTTP-contract fixtures for all 16 containerized services.

## Packaging

- The flat `src/` layout is now the `deepmarkpy` package (`pip install .`), with a `deepmark-benchmark` console script. `python src/run.py` keeps working through a deprecation shim.
- Python imports change accordingly: `from core.base_attack import ...` becomes `from deepmarkpy.core.base_attack import ...` (see `docs/MIGRATION.md`).
- Plugin discovery uses one module identity (`deepmarkpy.plugins.*`); the `sys.path` mutation is gone. Third-party plugin directories load via the new `--plugins_dir` flag or the `DEEPMARK_PLUGINS_DIR` environment variable, and import failures are recorded in `PluginManager.failed`.
- New additive CLI surface: `--plugins_dir` and `--report_dir` (default `./report`, unchanged behavior). All existing flags and values are unchanged.
- Container images install the package; behavior and the docker-compose workflow are unchanged.

## Plugin internals

- Every containerized plugin's inference logic lives in one `inference.py` module exposing a uniform `Engine` class behind a thin FastAPI `app.py` (see `docs/CONSUMING.md`). HTTP contracts are byte-identical.
- The `encodec` and `descript_audio_codec` attacks run as Docker services (ports `ENCODEC_PORT`/`DESCRIPT_AUDIO_CODEC_PORT`); PyTorch is no longer a host dependency.

## Known issues

- Known behavior quirks are intentionally preserved in this release and deferred to a later fix release.

### Fixed

- Resampling between rates whose reduced ratio has an upsampling factor above 16 (44.1, 22.05 and 11.025 kHz against 8, 16, 24, 32 and 48 kHz, among others) applies the windowed-sinc low-pass of the other rates at exact output positions, so a caller at these rates gets the channel a caller at 24 or 48 kHz gets, and `ResampleStage(zeros=...)` applies at these ratios too. 0.1.0 used a FIR and linear interpolation there. Every profile resamples between the caller's rate and 8 or 16 kHz on entry and exit, and for a 44.1 kHz caller:
  - a 44.1 → 8 → 44.1 kHz round trip was 1.9 dB down at 2 kHz, 4.4 dB at 3 kHz and 6.5 dB at 3.4 kHz, and 16 → 44.1 kHz was 2.9 dB down at 5 kHz and 6.3 dB at 7 kHz;
  - each hop shifted the signal by up to 51 µs, earlier going down and later going up, so the shifts cancelled only in a profile that leaves through the rate it entered at, with matching input and output rates; `voip_to_cellular_narrowband` (in at 16 kHz, out from 8 kHz) came out about 31 µs late even then;
  - the interpolation positions were computed in float32 and drifted: up to about 0.2 samples off after a minute of input and up to 4 samples after ten.

  Output changes wherever such a ratio is resampled: the simulator with an input or output rate of 44.1, 22.05 or 11.025 kHz, `load_audio` of a file at such a rate (including to the default 24 kHz, so `phonesim run` and `batch` on such files change), PESQ in `analyze_channel` at such a rate, and custom chains that resample or run a codec stage at such a rate. On 44.1 kHz speech through `pstn_narrowband` and `voip_g722_wideband` the difference from 0.1.0 is 16–27 dB below the output with a 44.1 kHz output rate, and 9.5–21 dB with a 24 kHz one, where 0.1.0's shifts did not cancel; through `voip_to_cellular_narrowband` it is 13–17 dB, and for `load_audio` to 24 kHz 20–24 dB below the signal. Resampling between 8, 16, 24, 32 and 48 kHz is unchanged, bit for bit.
- `ClockDriftStage` and `SpeedDriftStage` compute where each output sample falls in the input exactly (in float64, and in integer arithmetic through the new `dsp.linear_resize`). 0.1.0 computed those positions in float32, so their error grew along the signal: at 16 kHz, `ClockDriftStage` was up to 0.01 samples off a few seconds in and 0.09 after a minute, and from 2^23 samples (8.7 min) on its positions were whole samples; `SpeedDriftStage` was up to 0.09 samples off after a minute and 1.6 after ten. A run therefore changes, at any sample rate, when its drift stage draws a drift: every randomized run that draws at least 0.5 ppm of clock drift or any speed drift (only `stress_multi_transcode` has a speed-drift stage), and deterministic runs of custom drift stages whose deterministic draw is a drift, such as `ClockDriftStage(ppm=40)`. Deterministic runs of the built-in profiles (`randomize=False`, `--deterministic`) draw no drift and are unchanged at 8, 16, 24, 32 and 48 kHz. On 24 kHz speech, randomized runs differ from 0.1.0 by about 57–70 dB below the output for 5 s inputs, 37–46 dB for 60 s and 15–25 dB for 600 s.
- `NoiseStage(color="hum")` computes its time axis in float64; in float32 the hum's error grew from 60 dB below it after one minute to 35–40 dB below after ten. No profile uses it.
- `dsp.resample` returns an empty signal for an empty input instead of raising.

### Changed

- An unset output rate is the input rate. `PhoneCallSimulator` and `PhoneCallPipeline` without `output_sample_rate`, `build_profile` without `output_sr`, a config without `output_sr`, and `phonesim run` / `batch` without `--out-sr` return audio at the input rate. 0.1.0 resampled it to 24 kHz, so a caller at another input rate that did not set the output rate silently got audio at a different rate from its own. Set the output rate to 24000 to keep 0.1.0's output.
- Profile versions fix the stage chain and its parameters, not the arithmetic inside a stage: this release keeps every version although output changes (above). Output is reproducible for a given phonesim release, seed, profile version and codec build on one machine and torch thread count; phonesim 0.1.0 still regenerates 0.1.0 output.

### Deprecated

- `save_audio` without `sr` writes a 24 kHz header whatever rate the signal is at, now with a `FutureWarning`; from 0.3.0 `sr` is required.
- `analyze_channel` and `plot_channel` without `sample_rate` take the signals to be at 24 kHz, now with a `FutureWarning`; from 0.3.0 `sample_rate` is required.
- A `ResampleStage` whose `from_sr` disagrees with the rate the signal arrives at. `from_sr` was documented as a sanity check but never checked; the stage now warns (`FutureWarning`) and resamples from the signal's rate as before. From 0.3.0 this raises `ValueError`. `from_sr=None` takes any rate, and the built-in profiles' chains line up at every rate.

# Dev13 terminal-retirement evidence

`0.1.0.dev13` adds an authenticated read-only projection at
`GET /v1/leases/LEASE_ID/terminal-retirement` on the existing local API. It joins
the ready, unexpired host lease and retained handback journal with affirmative
Node retirement, dedicated-key rejection, saved cleanup, and current host/boot
identity. The response contains safe identity fields and retirement evidence,
without credentials, credential paths or file fingerprints. It grants no access
and does not attest activity after a customer has held root.

Every new terminal handback now reads affirmative same-org, exact-Node retirement
proof after the conditional Node deletion and before dedicated-key revocation.
An older interrupted `node_retired` journal can obtain the missing proof while
its key still exists. Missing or invalid proof preserves that key and keeps the
hold quarantined. An already-completed old journal without affirmative proof
remains ineligible for the new projection. There is no implicit database repair,
credential issuance, new retry, or timeout extension.

CPU checks cover the actual authenticated HTTP route, unchanged database state,
stale and conflicting evidence, normal retirement ordering, and persisted
pre-upgrade resume. Simulated remote responses and synthetic hardware do not
qualify the hosted retirement path. The release verification summary separately
records reproducible packaging and installed-artifact checks.

Fifteen runtime modules and the installer are byte-identical to dev12. Changes
are limited to `api.py`, `handback.py`, and version metadata; serving recipe
generation retains the same descriptors and accepts the new package version.
All earlier release assets and historical outcomes remain unchanged.

There remain **zero fully hardware-qualified production configurations**. This
release does not qualify native customer login, external provisioning or reimage,
post-customer isolation, or return to lending. The external owner still needs
independent physical-host, remote retirement and key-revocation verification.
See the [terminal return guide](terminal-native-return.md) and
[support matrix](support-matrix.md).

Verify all downloaded assets against `SHA256SUMS` before installation. Earlier releases remain unchanged.

Development prerelease with corrected first-run instructions: explicit installed executable paths, matching vLLM/SGLang generator and client lifecycles, a bounded health check, and clear credential choices before the first connection.

All 17 non-version runtime modules and the installer are byte-identical to dev11. Exact packaged commands were checked in a network-disabled Linux CPU container using synthetic loopback HTTP responses. No new GPU qualification is implied; historical results and failures retain their original release and environment bindings.

Use the source archive for the README, recipe generator and complete guides. See the attached release-dev12.md, verification-summary.json, support-matrix.md, release-manifest.json and SHA256SUMS for scope and exact assets. All older releases remain unchanged.

# Dev11 local dashboard usability

`0.1.0.dev11` improves the read-only local dashboard. The token form supports
Enter, controls show when a refresh is in progress, and duplicate refreshes
share a single pending operation. Status and errors have live announcement
regions, keyboard focus is visible, and focus returns to the initiating control
when disabling it caused the browser to lose focus. Moving focus elsewhere is
respected.

The browser bounds the complete inventory-and-status refresh, including response
bodies, to 120 seconds. A timeout restores the controls and reports an error;
it does not claim to cancel work already running on the server. Existing
30-second freshness and stale-data behavior continue while a refresh is pending
or fails. There is no new background polling. The token remains in browser
memory only, and the dashboard still sends only read requests.

Local Chromium checks exercised Enter, successful and failed refreshes,
duplicate submissions, recovery, stalled requests and response bodies, expiry
during a pending refresh, focus retention and narrow screens. Timeout checks
used controlled browser time rather than waiting 120 seconds of wall time.
The layout was checked at 320 CSS pixels with long resource identifiers.
These checks use local synthetic HTTP responses, not a GPU or a deployed
platform. Live-region markup is checked; no screen-reader audit is claimed.

# Dev10 permission freshness

`0.1.0.dev10` counts platform request time within the existing 20-second
permission freshness limit. Previously, a delayed response started a new
20-second window when it arrived. Enabled connection, explicit terms acceptance
and permission refresh now retain the request-start timestamp. An over-age
response or a backward/invalid request clock refuses authorization.

The change preserves exact enrolled-node identity, explicit opt-in, accepted
terms, workload policy, lease generations and normal cleanup requirements.
Persisted dev9 permission timestamps have no request-start provenance and are
denied until an ordinary fresh permission GET succeeds. The marker binds its
exact timestamp, so an older writer cannot preserve the marker while replacing
the timestamp. Connection settings, accepted consent and history are retained;
no renewed terms acceptance or database migration is required.

Observation-only requests continue to create no execution permission. A fresh
successful request can restore permission through the existing policy path;
it cannot release held ownership or revive a draining lease.

One focused regression uses the real local SQLite allocation and admission path
with an explicitly simulated platform response and clock. It fails on the dev9
code and passes on dev10: a response taking 19 seconds has no remaining validity
two seconds later, an ordinary fresh response recovers, and a response taking
21 seconds refuses permission. The 26 existing affected connection, observation
and CLI tests passed locally. An additional persisted-record regression checks
legacy, unknown and mismatched timestamp markers after restarting Connection;
a fresh GET restores admission without changing consent, policy revision or
event history. This is CPU implementation evidence, not a deployed
connected GPU or commercial-consent test.

# 0.4.3 — Prompt injection Block, Codex native patches, and Cursor and Devin prompts

A Fleet Block entry for prompt injection now stops the call in Claude Code
before it runs. A detection rule set to Block also stops a Codex edit made
with the native `apply_patch` tool, before its file is written, and a Cursor
or Devin prompt.

## Highlights

- **Claude Code sends tool results for prompt injection** (stacktrace
  ADR-0223). New `PostToolUse` and `PostToolUseFailure` hooks send the result
  of an MCP, `Read`, `Grep`, `Glob`, `Bash`, `WebFetch`, `WebSearch`, `Agent`,
  `Task` or other reading tool to the local daemon. The daemon keeps only
  keyed hashes of the values that a result names, and only while the
  organization has a Block entry for `stacktrace-injection-followed`. A later
  call that carries a value only a planted instruction named is denied
  before it runs, and the agent asks the person. The hook never blocks and
  prints nothing.
- **Claude Code sends `Read`, `Grep` and `Glob` calls to the policy hook.**
  `stacktrace-secret-path-read` already reads their paths, but the plugin did
  not send them. A Block entry now stops such a call before it runs.
- **Codex sends native patches to the Stacktrace hook.** The Codex
  `PreToolUse` matcher adds `apply_patch`. A detection rule with a Block
  entry stops a patch that writes a credential, plants a start-up command or
  changes an agent's settings. Before, the edit was written and the scan
  found it after the fact.
- **Cursor and Devin send prompts to the Stacktrace hook.** Cursor's
  `beforeSubmitPrompt` and Devin's `UserPromptSubmit` run the policy hook. A
  blocked Cursor prompt gets `continue: false`, and Cursor shows the reason.
  A failed or older CLI adds no block.

## Install

Claude Code:

```text
/plugin marketplace add stacktrace-ai/stacktrace-plugin
/plugin install stacktrace@stacktrace
```

Existing installations update with `claude plugin update stacktrace@stacktrace`
or with marketplace auto-update. Restart Claude Code to apply the update.

Cursor CLI:

```text
agent plugin marketplace add github.com/stacktrace-ai/stacktrace-plugin --git-ref v0.4.3
```

Codex CLI: follow the "Codex CLI policy hooks" section of the README. After
the update, review the Stacktrace hooks in `/hooks`, or run the installer
again, which trusts the installed Stacktrace hooks.

Devin: follow the "Devin policy hooks" section of the README, with the tag
`v0.4.3`.

## Compatibility

- **Prompt injection Block needs `stacktrace-cli` 0.25.0 or newer.** An older
  CLI ignores the tool results, so the rule's Block denies nothing. Upgrade
  the CLI before this plugin, then restart the daemon.
- **Each `Read`, `Grep` and `Glob` call in Claude Code now starts the hook
  twice**, before and after the call. Each start runs the CLI once.
- Before Claude Code 2.1.319, ending the turn with `Ctrl+Enter` while a tool
  runs skips the post-tool hook, so that result is not marked.
- **Codex stops running the Stacktrace `PreToolUse` hook after the update
  until you trust it again.** Its matcher changed, so Codex reports the hook
  as modified, and it runs only trusted hooks. Until then, no Codex tool call
  is decided. Review the hooks in `/hooks`, or run the installer again.
- Requires `stacktrace-cli` 0.23.0 or newer for native patch blocking. An
  older CLI gives no decision, and the patch continues.
- Cursor prompt blocking needs `stacktrace-cli` 0.22.0 or newer.
- Devin prompt blocking needs `stacktrace-cli` 0.24.0 or newer. No signed-in
  Devin session has confirmed that Devin stops a prompt on a block.
- The other `stacktrace-cli` and Claude Code minimums are the same as in 0.4.2.
- **Native patch blocking is verified only from Codex code mode.** The tests
  use Codex 0.166.0, where the model calls `tools.apply_patch` from code
  mode. A direct `apply_patch` call outside code mode is not tested.
- **Each Codex native patch now runs the hook.** The CLI sends the patch text
  to the local daemon. That text does not go to Fleet. Only the finding of a
  block does.

# 0.4.2 — Codex shell commands and prompts reach Fleet policy

A detection rule set to Block now stops a Codex shell command and a Codex
prompt, as it does in Claude Code.

## Highlights

- **Codex sends shell commands to the Stacktrace hook.** The Codex
  `PreToolUse` matcher adds `Bash`, the name Codex gives its shell tool at the
  hook, also for a patch sent through the shell. A detection rule with a Block
  entry, such as credential egress, stops the command before it runs.
- **Codex sends prompts to the Stacktrace hook.** A new `UserPromptSubmit`
  handler runs the same command. A blocked prompt reaches no model.
